title: The target is clear. The addressee depends on the version.
explanation: The maidservant declares a ban on the father. The base text does not say whom she addresses. Other versions add “to him”.

variants.label: Base text: “she said”
variants.note: The father is the target. The addressee stays unknown.

variants.label: Other version: “she said to him”
variants.note: The added pronoun supports the father as addressee in this version.

title: Brother in the printed text. Nephew in a proposed correction.
explanation: The printed phrase calls Hananya a brother of Hoshaya. Commentaries and parallel passages support reading “son of his brother”. Both sources remain saved.

variants.label: Printed wording
variants.note: A textual branch, preserved even when a correction is preferred.

variants.label: Commentary and parallel reading
variants.note: The parent has no personal name here, but still has a local person entry.

title: An objection and its answer need different speakers.
explanation: The earlier reading gave the quotation to Rav Oshaya. Published explanations read it as the discussion’s reply. The printed Hebrew leaves room to preserve the alternative.

variants.label: Reply reading
variants.note: The anonymous discussion cites the teacher. This supplies no personal meeting with Oshaya.

variants.label: Continuation reading
variants.note: The citation continues the objection. The internal speaker boundary remains interpretive.

title: Words that were not said can still be evidence.
explanation: The passage uses the missing formal address “Master” to support calling Yirmiya a student-colleague of Rav. A later quotation gives the formal wording instead.

variants.label: Focal passage
variants.note: Save the negative speech claim. Do not invent an event in which these words were spoken.

variants.label: Later quotation
variants.note: This witness includes the formal address. It does not supply the same argument for the relationship.

title: The same words can name a role or refer to a person.
explanation: The first “high priest” is a category in a legal rule. A later occurrence refers to the unnamed incumbent in the story. Attaching the person to the first occurrence was wrong.

variants.label: Legal rule
variants.note: A generic role in a legal scenario. No historical person is identified.

variants.label: Story
variants.note: A separate local person, even though his personal name is not given.

title: Two commentaries divide the same names differently.
explanation: One reading has Yohanan quote Yirmeya. Another starts a new chain at Yirmeya. The proposed identities of Yirmeya and Meisha differ too, so chronology cannot choose a reading before identity is checked.

variants.label: Printed links, retained by Guggenheimer
variants.note: Helbo’s connection to Shimon remains unspecified. These arrows show only the four explicit “in the name of” joins.

variants.label: Ohr LaYesharim’s reconstruction
variants.note: This reconstruction changes some joins and supplies others. Keep each change attached to its commentary or reported textual witness.

title: One extra word supplies an explicit teacher relationship.
explanation: Some versions have Yose call Hila “my teacher”. Others report Hila speaking to him but omit that title.

variants.label: Ketubot wording with “my teacher”
variants.note: The teacher link is explicit in this reading. Yose’s wider historical identity remains open.

variants.label: Parallel wording without that title
variants.note: The missing title does not prove that Hila was not his teacher. This version simply supplies less explicit evidence.

title: One sentence gives two links to a Rav Nachman.
explanation: “Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman said in the name of Rav Nachman.” The name gives a father. The report gives a source for the ruling. The text never says the two are the same man.

variants.label: Same man (one commentator)
variants.note: Yam shel Shelomoh reads the quoted Rav Nachman as the father. That is his reading, not the text.
edges: reports a ruling in the name of

variants.label: Two men named Rav Nachman
variants.note: No source says this. It stays open only because the text never says “his father”.
edges: reports a ruling in the name of

variants.label: Old pair table
variants.note: One “cites” label hid the family link.

title: The Talmud stops at a forecast. The English adds the marriages.
explanation: Rav Hisda's young daughter says she wants both men. Rava says he will be last. The Aramaic ends there. The marriages come from the translation's plain-text explanation and from later commentary.

variants.label: Aramaic text
variants.note: Both men sit before Rav Hisda. She wants both. Nobody marries in this passage.

variants.label: English plain text and commentary
variants.note: In the Davidson English these words are not bold, so they are the editor's explanation. Save them as that reading, not as the Talmud's words.

variants.label: Old pair table
variants.note: The name finder cut “Rami bar Hama” down to “Hama”.

title: All three really met. The honour was only in one man's head.
explanation: Mar Zutra meets Rava and Rav Safra on the road. In the printed text he thinks they came out to greet him; they had not. Who says the last line depends on the version.

variants.label: Printed text: the meeting
variants.note: Mar Zutra's belief is a thought, not a link. Rava's rebuke names no listener; his words show it is Rav Safra.

variants.label: Last line: Rava
variants.note: The Davidson English and Steinsaltz Hebrew say so, but they are one project, so they count once. The Rif's wording is a bracketed later quotation of uncertain standing.

variants.label: Last line: Rav Safra
variants.note: The printed Aramaic has one “he said to him” that may cover both sentences. No commentator reads it this way.
